St Louis County by the numbers

Where does a deed for a St. Louis County house get filed?

It goes to the St. Louis County Recorder of Deeds in Clayton, and only when the parcel lies outside the City of St. Louis. The counter is on South Central Avenue (number 41). The county's recorder page gives (314) 615-7100 for calls and shows the office open Monday through Thursday only, from 8 until 3:30.

Besides deeds, the same staff file subdivision plats, federal and state tax liens and other written instruments touching real or personal property, and they issue marriage licenses. Anything recorded there is open to public research, and written questions can go to Recorder@stlouiscountymo.gov at the full address 41 South Central Avenue, Clayton, MO 63105. For a sale in Florissant, Chesterfield, Ballwin or any other municipality in the county, the closing agent usually takes the signed deed to this office, so a seller seldom visits in person.

What will the county bill me to put a deed on record?

The county's price page sets $26 for page one and $3 for every page after it. A document that ignores the state layout rules draws a further $25. Anyone who files electronically may pay a vendor's own charges on top.

The layout rules come from RSMo 59.310. A recorder may turn away a paper that fails them, or accept it with the surcharge. A deed packet for this office typically needs:

  • single-sided pages on white or pale paper, loose rather than bound;
  • type of at least eight points, in black or dark ink, with legible signatures and typed names beneath them;
  • three clear inches at the top of the first sheet, reserved for the recorder's certification, and three-quarters of an inch around the other edges;
  • on that first sheet, under the margin: title, date, every grantor with marital status, every grantee, statutory addresses, and the legal description.

Pay too much and the county's overpayment page says a check comes back only if the excess tops $10. Smaller overages go into the county's general fund.

Is the county office the same as the one in the city?

No. In 1877 the voters of St. Louis chose to separate from the county, and the two have kept separate land records since. A house a few blocks east or west of the boundary can therefore belong to a different office.

The city's recorder works from City Hall, Room 126, at 1200 Market Street, and its land records page publishes its own prices. Look at the parcel's address first, because a deed sent to the wrong office will not help your closing.

Can I mail my deed in, or does it have to be filed online?

Mailing works. Send or hand over the original notarized deed, with a check or money order made out to ROD, to the Clayton address. The filing instructions promise the original back within a week of recording. Electronic filing runs through the third-party vendors named on the county's e-recording page.

That page tells businesses that want to file electronically to contact a vendor and set up service. A seller with one deed rarely needs that, and the title company handling the sale will normally take care of the recording and pass along a copy.

One question the county pages leave open is whether any charge besides recording applies to your particular deed. The price page lists recording fees only, so put the question to the Recorder's office on (314) 615-7100 or to the closing agent before you sign.

What if the recorder will not accept my deed?

The statute says a rejected paper goes back to whoever brought it, with the reason written out. Once the problem is fixed, you can present it again. The same law allows a non-conforming paper to be recorded for the $25 add-on instead of being refused.

Some papers are exempt from the layout rules and may still be recorded. The list in the statute includes documents signed before January 1, 2002, papers executed outside the United States, certified copies, and anything where an original party has died or is otherwise incapacitated. An heir selling a parent's house could fall into that last group, so tell the title company early.

Hold on to the stamped copy afterward. The top three inches carry the recorder's certification, which makes the copy your proof that the deed reached the record.

How do I order a copy of my deed or look up an old one?

Order a certified copy online from the county's vendor, or go in person. The counter takes cards only. According to the copy instructions, pages cost $2 for the first and $1 for each after, a typical printed deed comes to $5 plus a convenience charge, and each certification adds $1.

  • The web search reaches recorded deeds through 1974.
  • If you bought before 1974, book an appointment for a deed search in Clayton.
  • You may also book one if you would rather search on site.
  • State law caps what a recorder may charge for a paper copy of a recorded instrument at $2 for the first page and $1 for each later page, which matches the county's posted copy price.

Pull a recent copy before you list. The buyer's title company will check names and the legal description against it.

What does the county look like on paper?

St. Louis County lies in eastern Missouri, with the Missouri River along its north edge, the Meramec River along most of the south, and the Mississippi and the City of St. Louis to the east. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table estimates 990,911 residents for July 2025 on 507.88 square miles of land, with 448,637 homes counted.

Owners live in 69.2% of occupied homes. Owners rate the middle house at $276,800 in the 2020 to 2024 survey, middle household income is $82,936, and monthly rent in the middle is $1,209. Eighty-seven municipal governments operate in the county, and roughly one resident in three lives in an unincorporated area where the county itself handles zoning and code enforcement. Twenty-three public school systems cover the county, among them Clayton, Parkway, Rockwood and Webster Groves.

The county's 2023 financial report, as summarized on Wikipedia, names Washington University (19,617 employees), Boeing Defense, Space and Security (15,796) and Mercy Healthcare (15,084) as its biggest employers. The Special School District of St. Louis County, which runs schools for students with disabilities, is another large local employer with 5,890 staff.

A deed for a house in Clayton and one for a house in Wildwood are filed at the same counter, though each municipality governs its own streets. Ask city hall about local steps before you list.

More questions about St. Louis County, MO Recorder of Deeds

Where do I find the St. Louis County recorder?

At 41 South Central Avenue in Clayton, MO 63105. The county gives (314) 615-7100 and Recorder@stlouiscountymo.gov, and the doors are open Monday to Thursday from 8 to 3:30.

Recording charge for a deed here?

Twenty-six dollars for the first page and three for each page that follows, with a $25 add-on for a paper that breaks the Missouri format rules. Vendors who handle e-recording can charge extra.

Will the county take a deed by post?

Yes. Mail the original notarized deed and a check or money order payable to ROD to the Clayton office. The county returns the original within a week of recording.

My house is in St. Louis city. Do I file in Clayton?

No. The City of St. Louis keeps its own land records at City Hall, Room 126, and charges its own prices. Clayton handles only parcels in the county.

How far back does the online deed search go?

Recorded deeds can be searched through 1974. A property bought before that year calls for an appointment at the Clayton office.

Where is the Jackson County, MO Recorder of Deeds office?

The Recorder of Deeds works from one place only, the Historic Truman Courthouse at 112 W. Lexington, Suite 30, in Independence, MO 64050. Walk-in service runs weekdays from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m., with county holidays off. Call 816-881-4483 or write to records@jacksongov.org.

The Kansas City courthouse at 415 E. 12th St. handles tax payments, but the county states the recorder is located only in Independence. Mail submissions go to the same suite. Documents also arrive through electronic filing, which banks, title companies and law firms use, and Jackson County accepts electronic signatures and notarization through that route and at the walk-in and mail desk.

What does the recorder do for a house sale in Jackson County?

The office reviews and indexes each document before it enters the public record. It checks that the paper meets the minimum recording requirements. It does not fill out forms, help owners complete them, or check the content, so questions about wording belong with a title agent or a Missouri attorney.

The buyer's deed ends up in this office's index, and so does the lender's release after a payoff. The county says it records nearly 100 types of documents.

  • Deeds and deeds of trust
  • Releases and assignments of mortgages
  • Uniform Commercial Code real estate filings
  • State and federal tax liens and releases
  • Notices of mechanic's lien
  • Plats and surveys

What is the price of recording a deed in Jackson County?

A standard deed runs $23 on page one and $3 on each page that follows. The county posted a new fee schedule, and any document received on or after August 28, 2026 falls under it, whether it came by e-recording or by mail, regardless of postmark. That date has now passed, so the schedule below is the one in force.

Where does a Jackson County recording fee go?

Out of the $23 first-page charge, $8 goes to the State of Missouri and $15 stays in the county. The state share is split among the Secretary of State Local Preservation Fund, the State Surveyor Fund, the State Housing Trust Fund and the State Statutory County Recorder's Fund. The county share is divided between the General Fund, the Recorder's Fee Fund, a County Homeless Fund and a Technology Fund. Each added page at $3 goes entirely to the county's General Fund.

A recording line on a settlement statement is a flat amount tied to page count, so a longer deed with exhibits costs a few dollars more.

How can I pay the Jackson County recorder?

By mail, make the check payable to the Recorder of Deeds Department. At the recording office you can pay with cash, check, debit or credit card. A debit or credit card adds a 2.75% merchant processing fee on the entire transaction, so a large batch of documents costs noticeably more by card than by check.

Certified copies of deeds can be ordered online through the county's Aumentum portal at aumentumweb.jacksongov.org. A certified marriage license copy costs $10, and a plain request by mail needs a personal check or money order for that amount.

What must a deed look like to be recorded in Jackson County?

Page one must carry the document title, its date, every grantor with marital status, every grantee, any statutory addresses and the legal description, all below a three-inch top margin. This mirrors Missouri statute 59.310, which also calls for at least three-quarters of an inch on the other sides, type no smaller than eight-point, dark ink, and white or light paper of at least twenty-pound weight.

  • Pages are printed on one side only and are not permanently bound.
  • Signatures are in dark ink with the name typed or printed beneath.
  • A document that misses the format rules can still be recorded for an extra $25 under the statute.
  • The recorder returns a rejected document with an explanation.

The county also recommends leaving out nonessential personal information, and it publishes a page on redacting personal information.

Does every Kansas City address record in Jackson County?

Not every one. Kansas City is the county's largest city and a co-seat, but its limits also reach into Platte and Clay counties and a small part of Cass County. A parcel north of the Missouri River can belong to a neighboring county's recorder, so check the county on the tax bill before you send a deed here.

Inside Jackson County, the same Independence office records deeds for Lee's Summit, Blue Springs, Raytown, Grandview, Grain Valley, Oak Grove, Lone Jack and the other cities. Lee's Summit alone is described by the county as home to more than 86,000 residents, so volume at one office is high. Submit complete packets, with the first-page information in place, and you reduce the odds of a return.

For an estate sale or a deed from a trust, the recorder will check only format, so sort out authority to sign with the attorney or title agent before the packet leaves your hands. Ask your title company whether it files electronically, since the county page says title firms and law offices use that portal.

How do I guard against deed fraud in Jackson County?

The recorder links an alert service at propertyfraudalert.com. Owners who sign up get a notice whenever a document is recorded against a property they own. A seller who plans to keep other parcels, or an heir managing an inherited home, can watch for a forged deed that way.

The recorder's page also links a document search for county records, and certified copies of anything found there are ordered through the Aumentum portal.

What else should a Jackson County seller check before closing?

Tax is the common loose end. The Department of Collection explains that an unpaid real estate balance follows the parcel to the buyer, so have the title agent confirm what is owed before the deed is filed. A military discharge recorded here is free, and a copy request needs a notarized form.

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show that 59.1% of county households own and that the middle owned home is valued at $230,500, so the typical deed here conveys real money. For tax questions, see the county's property tax guide on this site, and call the Assessment office to update the owner and mailing address after a sale.

More questions about Jackson County, MO Recorder of Deeds

What will the Jackson County recorder charge me for a deed?

It charges $23 for page one and $3 for each page after. The schedule applies to documents received on or after August 28, 2026. Paying by card adds 2.75% on the whole transaction.

Is there a Kansas City counter for deed recording?

No. The county states the Recorder of Deeds is located only at the Historic Truman Courthouse, 112 W. Lexington, Suite 30, Independence, MO 64050. Mail works too, and title companies can e-record.

Will the recorder prepare my deed?

No. The office reviews and indexes documents but will not complete forms or check them beyond the minimum recording requirements. A title agent or Missouri attorney can draft it.

What if my Jackson County deed breaks the format rules?

The recorder can reject it and return it with a reason, or record it for an extra $25 under Missouri statute 59.310. Fix margins, type size and first-page details to avoid either outcome.

Where can I order a certified deed copy from Jackson County?

Order it online through the county's Aumentum portal at aumentumweb.jacksongov.org. The fee page lists $1 for certification and $2 for the first copied page plus $1 for each additional page.

Boone County by the numbers

What does the Boone County Recorder of Deeds do?

The office keeps the public record of land transactions in Boone County, and it also issues marriage licenses. Deeds, deeds of trust, releases, easements, plats, surveys, restrictions, cemetery deeds, wills, road rights of way and affidavits all end up in its indexes. For a home seller in Columbia, Ashland, Centralia or anywhere else in the county, the closing is not complete until the deed reaches this office.

The index of deeds and deeds of trust reaches back to 1821, and computerized real estate records start in 1975. A separate index covers releases and assignments, and state and federal tax liens are indexed by taxpayer name, with computerized lien records starting in 1985. Marriage records on computer begin in 1973. The office phone is 573-886-4345, according to the fee schedule page.

Copies of every deed and deed of trust go to the Assessor, so the recorded document is what updates ownership for the next tax bill.

What does it cost to record a deed in Boone County?

A standard real estate document costs $26.00 for the first page and $3.00 for each page after that, based on the county's posted fee schedule. The statute listing recorder fees, RSMo 59.310, shows a base of $5.00 for the first page and $3.00 for each following page, so the county's figure includes charges beyond that base. Pay the number the Recorder posts, and call 573-886-4345 if a closing agent quotes something different.

How do cards and overpayments work at the Boone County Recorder?

Card users pay a $1.55 fee on transactions up to $66.00 and 2.35 percent on anything larger. Those charges sit on top of the recording fee.

The Recorder keeps an overpayment of up to $10.00. The stated reason is speed: documents can be recorded in priority order without being bounced for a small shortfall, as long as the payment is not below the statutory fee. Anything beyond that is receipted and deposited. A request to get an overpayment back must be written and reach the office within 30 days of recording, and the Recorder then has 30 days to decide. UCC fixture filings are the exception, since overpayments on those are never refunded.

What must a Boone County deed include to be recorded?

The Recorder's requirements page mirrors the format rules in state law. A document that follows them records as standard. One that does not still records, but as a non-standard document, and a $25.00 penalty is added to the normal fee under RSMo 59.310.

  • Title and date of the document on the first page, below a blank 3-inch top margin.
  • Names of every grantor with marital status, plus the grantees, on the first page.
  • Grantee mailing address and the legal description of the land on the first page.
  • Grantor signature, with the name typed or printed under each signature.
  • Notary acknowledgment with signature and seal, stamped in blank space rather than over text.
  • Letter-size paper, margins of at least three-quarters of an inch elsewhere, and type no smaller than 8 point.

A recording certificate is stamped in the top margin when the document is accepted. A rejected document comes back with a written reason. Documents signed before 2002, military separation papers, papers signed abroad, certified copies, documents where a party has died and court-formatted judgments are exempt from the layout rules, according to the statute.

Which closing papers have special rules in Boone County?

A few document types ask for extra items, and they matter when a seller is paying off a loan or buying out of foreclosure.

  • A release deed must list the book and page of the deed of trust being released. If that deed of trust was recorded before January 1, 1986, the original note, marked paid, has to come along, or an affidavit of lost note from the maker and holder.
  • A trustee's deed after foreclosure must show the book and page of the foreclosed deed of trust, and the original identified note is required when that deed of trust was recorded before 1986.
  • An assignment of deed of trust should list the book and page of the instrument being assigned.
  • Fixture filings under the Uniform Commercial Code stay with the county, while other UCC filings go to the Secretary of State.

The Recorder does not draft deeds or answer legal questions. A title company or attorney handles preparation, and the Recorder's office handles filing and retrieval.

What should a seller check before a deed goes to the Recorder?

Most recording problems come from small gaps that a closing agent can catch in advance. A few minutes of review saves the $25.00 non-standard charge and avoids a returned document.

  • Confirm every grantor name matches the prior deed and that marital status is stated.
  • Check that the legal description is on page one, or that page one points to the page where it appears.
  • Leave the top three inches clear and keep notary seals out of the margins.
  • Ask whether a lien, such as a state or federal tax lien indexed by taxpayer name, will need a discharge recorded at $7.50.
  • Request a certified or plain copy afterward, at $1.00 per page plus $1.00 for the certification.

Marriage licenses, which cost $53.00 at this office, are handled at the same counter but have nothing to do with a house sale.

How does the Recorder connect to the Boone County tax bill?

Because the Recorder passes every deed to the Assessor, the date a deed is recorded can decide whose name appears on the next tax bill. The Collector notes that a closing on or after October 1 may produce a bill in the seller's name at the old address unless the buyer reports the sale. Sellers should ask the title company to confirm the deed was recorded, then tell the Collector or Assessor about the new owner.

Fees collected here go to the County Treasurer, apart from special fees forwarded directly to the state each month. The Recorder also files a monthly fee report with the Auditor and settles up yearly with the County Commission.

What is the housing market like behind Boone County deeds?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table lists 84,371 housing units in the county for 2025 and a median value of $272,800 for owner-occupied homes, the highest of the three Missouri counties compared there. The owner-occupied rate is 57.7 percent, median gross rent is $1,088, and 787 building permits were issued in 2025.

Those figures mean a steady flow of filings: sales, refinances, releases after payoffs and new subdivision plats. Columbia, with the University of Missouri, anchors most of that activity, and the Recorder's separate plat and survey fees reflect the platting that growth brings.

More questions about Boone County, MO Recorder of Deeds

How much does the Boone County Recorder charge for a standard deed?

$26.00 for the first page and $3.00 for each added page, per the county's fee schedule. A non-standard document costs $51.00 for the first page.

What happens if my deed is not in standard format?

It is recorded as non-standard, and a $25.00 penalty is added to the regular fee under RSMo 59.310. Following the margin, signature and notary rules avoids that charge.

Can I get an overpayment refunded?

Only in some cases. The Recorder keeps overpayments up to $10.00, and larger ones can be requested back in writing within 30 days of recording. UCC fixture filing overpayments are not refunded.

Does the Recorder prepare deeds for homeowners?

No. The office files and indexes documents and helps people search records, but legal drafting belongs to an attorney or title company.

How far back do Boone County land records go?

The general index reaches back to 1821, and computerized real estate records begin in 1975. Call 573-886-4345 for help with older books.

When a Platte County house sells, the deed to the buyer is recorded here, and so is the release that a lender files after its loan is paid off.

Uniform Commercial Code filings are not part of this office's work, because the Missouri Secretary of State has taken them since July 1, 2001. Only the DD214 disclaimer form needs a formal request. For other documents, you can phone or email and staff will pull them without a Sunshine request.

The custodian of records, Travis Youmans, takes any formal request at extension 3326 of the main number. The county notes that real estate and marriage records are public, while divorce records sit with the Circuit Clerk. Marriage license applications are taken from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

What are the recording fees at the Platte County recorder?

Expect $26 for the first page and $3 for every page after it when the document meets the standards. A statewide fee increase took effect on August 28, 2026, and the county says it touched recorded documents, marriage licenses and plats. That date is behind us, so the schedule below is the one in use. The fee page adds that overpayments are not refunded, which makes a phone call for the exact total worth the time.

A document that releases or assigns more than one item adds $5 for each extra item. The county site also lists a $53 marriage license fee, charged in exact cash or by card with a convenience fee. Source: Platte County Recorder Fees.

What turns a Platte County deed into a non-standard document?

Missing the Recorders Association of Missouri layout rules adds a $25 charge, which is exactly the gap between $26 and $51 on the first page. The rules date from January 1, 2002, and a title company or attorney will normally have them built into the deed form. A seller drafting a deed alone should check each item.

  • Letter-size paper that is white or light, 20-pound, without logos or watermarks.
  • Dark ink on one side, with type of at least 8 points.
  • The top 3 inches of page one left empty for the recorder's stamp, and three-quarter inch margins elsewhere.
  • A typed, stamped or printed name under every signature.
  • No tape or staples holding attachments to a page, other than a secure bar-coded label.

Page one must show the title, the date, each grantor with marital status, each grantee, statutory addresses and the legal description, and the words grantor and grantee must appear so the instrument can be indexed. A street address is not accepted as a legal description. See the county formatting page.

Which Platte County documents skip the formatting rules?

Several kinds of paper are exempt and pay only the per-page fee. Documents signed before January 1, 2002 are one group. The others are military separation papers, documents signed outside the United States, certified copies, judgments or papers shaped to court rules, and fixture filings on national approved forms. A document is also exempt when one of the original parties has died or is incapacitated.

Any cover sheet is optional, but if one is used it is recorded as page one and must have the 3-inch top margin and the first-page information. A paper sent in for re-recording needs a new first page or cover sheet that meets the same rules. Rejected documents come back with a reason stated.

Can I search or get alerts on Platte County records online?

Yes. The recorder's iRecord portal at plattemo.icounty.com handles searches, and the same site runs a free Record Notification Service. You register for a free account, confirm the email link, choose your criteria, and the system sends a message whenever a matching deed is recorded.

An owner can set the alert on their own name. The county adds that its data is not official and does not replace advice from a licensed professional. Online search pricing belongs to the portal, so ask the office or read the site before relying on any number.

Does a Platte County deed trigger a transfer tax?

The recorder's published schedule lists recording, copy and plat charges and has no line for a transfer tax. For tax advice on a sale, a title company or Missouri attorney is the right call, and the recorder at (816) 858-3326 can tell you what the office itself collects when it accepts a deed.

Property tax is a separate matter. The Platte County Collector bills it, with statements due on receipt and delinquent after December 31. The Assessor's office also lists a sales validation and education coordinator at (816) 858-1256, which is a useful number when a sale price needs to be explained to the county.

How busy is the Platte County recording market?

Platte County is part of the Kansas City metro area and is far larger than Pike County and Polk County. Census QuickFacts counts 114,400 residents and 47,969 housing units for July 1, 2025. A typical owned home is worth $345,100, owners occupy 67.4 percent of homes and 425 building permits were issued in 2025.

The county was organized on December 31, 1838, and the courthouse at Platte City carries a National Register listing. The recorder's staff includes a chief of staff, an assistant chief deputy and two deputy recorders, and a transparency portal posts the office's receipts. Because new documents are accepted only until 4 p.m., send a deed early in the day. Source: Census QuickFacts.

More questions about Platte County, MO Recorder of Deeds

It costs $26.00, and every added page costs $3.00. A document that misses the formatting standards costs $51.00 for the first page.

When can I file a document with the Platte County recorder?

Bring it between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. on a weekday. The office stays open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. for searches and copies.

What address do I use to send a deed for recording in Platte County?

Use the Recorder of Deeds, 415 Third St., Room 035, Platte City, MO 64079. Call (816) 858-3326 to confirm the total, because overpayments are not refunded.

How can I be told when a deed is recorded in Platte County?

Register for a free account at plattemo.icounty.com and set your criteria in the Record Notification Service. The system emails you when a matching deed reaches the office.

Does the Platte County recorder file UCC statements?

No. The Missouri Secretary of State has taken UCC filings since July 1, 2001. A real estate fixture filing on the approved form with the required addendum is priced at $26.00 for the first page.

What will the Clay County recorder decline to do?

State statute bars the office from searching for liens or saying whether one exists. Use the public computer at the office or hire a title company to run the search. A recorded deed also stays as it is. Adding or removing a name takes a new deed, prepared and recorded at the going rate.

  • Sale prices: these are not public record here, though the Assessor may give you the area's market value.

Paying off a mortgage records a release of the deed of trust. The release is not proof of ownership, since the deed from your seller is the document that shows you own the home. Owners occupy 69.5% of homes, the owner-occupied median value over 2020 to 2024 is $275,600 and median household income is $88,468. Renters pay a median $1,243, workers commute 22.8 minutes on average, and 297 building permits were issued in 2025.

Cities and towns include Liberty, Gladstone, Excelsior Springs, Smithville, Kearney, North Kansas City, Pleasant Valley, Claycomo and Missouri City. School districts serving the county are Liberty 53, North Kansas City 74, Kearney R-I, Smithville R-II, Excelsior Springs 40 and the elementary district at Missouri City. Interstates 29, 35 and 435 cross the county, along with US 69, 71 and 169.

Whatever town your house is in, the same Liberty office files the deed. Ask the closing attorney or title company who will deliver it, so it arrives ahead of the 4:00 p.m. cutoff.

$26.00 for page one and $3.00 for each added page, with $25.00 more for a non-standard document. These amounts include the flat $2.00 statewide increase effective August 28, 2026. Confirm page counts and card fees at 816-407-3550.

Until what time can a deed be filed in Clay County?

Until 4:00 p.m. on weekdays. The office stays open to 5:00 p.m. but takes no recordings after 4:00. It is at 1 Courthouse Square in Liberty, with a PO Box 238 mailing address.

Is a Clay County deed searchable by street address?

No. Records are indexed by name, not location. Get the book and page from the Clay County Assessor's real estate division, then use the recorder's online search or call the office. Online viewing is free once you register, while copies are paid.

Can the recorder fix a name or legal description on a deed that is already recorded?

No. A recorded document is a permanent record and cannot be edited. To change the title, a new deed or corrective document has to be prepared by you or an attorney and recorded at the current fee.

Is there a transfer tax line on the Clay County fee schedule?

The schedule lists recording, copy, certification, plat, lien and marriage license charges, and no transfer tax. Ask the Recorder at 816-407-3550 or your title company about any other cost tied to a particular closing.

More questions about Greene County, MO Recorder of Deeds

4:00 PM on a business day. Papers presented after that are recorded starting at 8:00 AM the next business day.

From the Greene County Assessor, Room 35 at 940 N Boonville Ave, or from its Public Access website. The recorder cannot search by street address.

Under that blank strip, page one has to carry the document title and date, each grantor with marital status, each grantee, required addresses and the legal description. A document that misses these rules can still go on record for an extra $25. Older deeds signed before 2002, certified copies and papers executed abroad escape the format rules altogether.

A rejected document comes back to the person who submitted it with a written reason, so a mistake costs time more than money.

How do I search Callaway County land records?

You can view recorded documents online at callawaymo.icounty.com. The Recorder's page says printing is available through subscriptions at several levels, and you can call the office for the options. The page also points to DeedWatch, a notification service run by the county's records vendor, which can alert an owner whenever a new document is filed under that name.

That alert is useful for a seller who has inherited a house or who shares a title with a relative, because it shows a lien, a release or a new deed soon after it is filed. It can also surface a filing you did not expect before a buyer's title company finds it.

The county also offers free GIS maps for the public, listed on its home page, which help with parcel lines on rural lots outside Fulton.

Which other Callaway County offices matter when I sell?

Three more offices share the courthouse at 10 E. 5th Street. The Collector's page gives their weekday hours as 8 to 4:30, closed on state holidays.

  • The Collector, Sarah Gladman, at 573-642-0747, bills and takes property tax payments. Per the county FAQ, statements are mailed during the final week of October.
  • The Assessor, Jody Paschal, values more than 26,000 parcels. Real property calls go to 573-642-0768, and personal property to 573-642-0766.
  • The County Clerk handles Board of Equalization appeals.

The Assessor's own page says field crews gather data in marked vehicles, wear safety vests with body cameras and county ID, and knock first. They take outside photos, may ask about a finished basement or the number of bathrooms, and never ask to come inside. State law puts the Board of Equalization filing cutoff on the second Monday of July. The Assessor's 2026 notice named July 8 at 5 p.m. instead, so ask the Clerk each year for the date that applies.

Back taxes or an open lien on the house should go to the title company early, so the payoff appears on the first draft of the settlement.

More questions about Callaway County, MO Recorder of Deeds

Where is a Callaway County deed filed?

At the Recorder of Deeds, 10 E. 5th Street, Fulton, MO 65251. The register closes at 4:00 in the afternoon. Call 573-642-0787 to ask how to submit it.

What is the Callaway County recording fee?

The statute sets $5 and $3 as the recorder's base, other statutory fees are added, and a $2 statewide increase began August 28, 2026. Cole and Camden Counties post $26 for page one, so request the current Callaway sheet.

Can I look up a Callaway County deed online?

Yes. Recorded documents can be viewed at callawaymo.icounty.com, and the Recorder sells subscriptions if you want to print them. The office can also explain what each level includes.

Why would the Recorder reject my deed?

The usual reasons are format problems under RSMo 59.310: a margin smaller than three inches at the top of page one, small or faint type, signatures without printed names, or missing grantor and grantee details. The office sends the document back with a written reason.

Is there a Callaway County transfer tax?

The fee list in RSMo 59.310 carries no transfer tax, only charges by page and document type. Confirm the total for your own deed with the Recorder at 573-642-0787 or with your title company.

Cass County by the numbers

What does the Cass County Recorder of Deeds do?

The Recorder of Deeds in Harrisonville records, indexes and preserves every land transaction in Cass County. That includes deeds, deeds of trust, release deeds, plats, surveys, powers of attorney, deed restrictions, state and federal tax liens and UCC fixture filings. The same office issues marriage licenses and records military discharge papers at no charge.

Mike Medsker holds the office. He was elected in November 2010 and returned in 2014, 2018 and 2022. Recording matters to a seller because RSMo 442.400 says an unrecorded instrument is valid only between the parties and anyone with actual notice. A deed that stays in a drawer does not protect the buyer against the rest of the world.

Where is the Cass County Recorder's office and how do I submit a deed?

The office is at 102 E. Wall St., Harrisonville, MO 64701, and its page lists hours from 8 a.m. until 4 p.m. on weekdays. The recorder's contact box gives 816-380-8118, while the county directory lists 816-380-8123 for the same office, so use whichever connects. The staff cannot draft or prepare documents for you. Cass County sends that work to a title company or a real estate attorney.

  • In person or by mail at the Wall Street address, with the correct fee.
  • Electronic recording through the iCounty portal. You sign a registration packet with the Recorder, mail it to Wall Street or email it to the address on the county's e-recording page, and pay by ACH through the portal.
  • ACH payments are refused for documents in delinquent status.
  • Free online document search once you register on the county site.

Cass County also runs a fraud alert system at casscounty.com/fraud. Anyone can sign up to be notified when a document carrying their name or business name is recorded.

How much does recording a deed in Cass County run?

Fees come from state law plus the county's own formatting rule. The base charge in RSMo 59.310 is per page, and RSMo 59.319 adds a flat user fee on every recorded instrument. The county's fee page links to the current posted schedule, so check it before mailing a check.

First page of a deed or instrument$5RSMo 59.310
Each page after the first$3RSMo 59.310
User fee on each instrument$6RSMo 59.319, version effective August 28, 2026

Each book and page reference beyond the first on a release or assignment$5Cass County recorder FAQ
Copy of a recorded instrument$1 per pageCass County recorder FAQ

A three-page deed in proper format costs $11 in page charges alone: $5 for page one and $3 for each of the other two. The user fee comes on top of that.

How must a deed be formatted for the Cass County recorder?

Cass County applies the formatting standards in effect since January 1, 2002. Documents signed before that date, military separation papers, documents executed outside the United States, certified copies, documents where an original party has died or is incapacitated, court-formatted judgments and national-form UCC fixture filings are exempt.

  • 8.5 by 11 inch white or light paper, at least 20 pound, printed on one side, black or dark ink, type no smaller than 8 point.
  • A blank top margin of 3 inches on the first page only, kept for the Recorder's certification, and at least three quarters of an inch on all other margins.
  • Signatures in dark ink with the name typed, printed or stamped underneath.
  • On the first page below the 3 inch margin: the document title, date, grantors and their marital status, grantees, any statutory addresses and the legal description.
  • Parties labeled with the words Grantor or Grantee so they can be indexed. The filer, not the office, makes those labels.

A cover page is optional, but if you use one it takes the same top margin and first page items. Re-recording a document needs a new cover sheet, new signatures and a fresh notarization.

Why does the Cass County recorder reject documents?

A rejected document comes back with the reason written out. The office lists the usual causes on its FAQ page, and most are fixable before you submit.

  • The fee is wrong.
  • The first page lacks the required designations.
  • Text sits inside the margins.
  • Signatures are missing a typed name or an acknowledgment.
  • A document affecting land has no proper legal description. A street address does not count.
  • A transfer of an interest in land has no mailing address for the grantee.
  • The copy is too faint to reproduce.
  • A release or assignment cites several book and page numbers without the extra $5 each.

Blanket assignments are not accepted. Because a rejection costs days, many sellers let the title company handle submission.

How fast does Cass County record a deed, and what does the public see?

The recorder states a turnaround of same day to 24 hours for real estate recordings, not counting holidays and weekends. Documents go back to the person who submitted them, often a lender or servicer. After a payoff, the lender usually files only a release deed, one to two pages long. The deed to a purchased house normally reaches the buyer at closing.

Some limits are worth knowing. Recorded real estate documents do not show the sale price. The office does not phone out closing details such as book, page or recording time, and it does not run lien searches, citing state law. Liens can also sit with the court or the Collector. For closing information, ask the title insurer, lender or agent. Anyone can see a recorded instrument on the public computers at the Harrisonville office.

What happens to property tax when a Cass County house sells?

The Collector of Revenue, Chris Molendorp, bills Cass County real estate from 2725 Cantrell Road in Harrisonville (816-380-8377, weekdays, opening at 8 and closing at 4:30). Bills go out in November and are due by December 31, judged by the U.S. postmark. Unpaid balances accrue penalties that can reach 25 percent in the first year of delinquency.

  • Taxes are a lien that stays with the land, so a new owner is liable for unpaid back taxes.
  • The county says taxes are generally prorated between buyer and seller at closing, and no money goes to the Collector at the sale.
  • A bill may still be issued in the seller's name until the Collector or Assessor learns of the new owner. A seller who receives one should send the buyer's name and address to the Collector.
  • Assessment ratios run 19 percent of market value for homes, 32 for commercial parcels and 12 for farmland.
  • Land with unpaid tax is offered at the annual tax sale, held on the fourth Monday in August at 10 a.m. The 2027 sale is set for Monday, August 23, 2027.

The Cass Assessor sets the value that the tax rate is applied to. The Collector has no power to raise or lower levies set by school, fire, library and hospital boards.

How large is the Cass County housing market?

Cass County sits in western Missouri, within the Kansas City area. Harrisonville holds the courthouse, and the county borders Jackson County to the north and Miami and Johnson counties in Kansas to the west. These Census Bureau QuickFacts figures cover the county as a whole.

  • The mid-2025 Census estimate is 115,859 people, up from 107,824 at the 2020 count.
  • Housing units in 2025: 48,259, with 75.6 percent of homes owner-occupied.
  • Owner-occupied homes had a middle value of $292,400 in the 2020 to 2024 survey.
  • Median gross rent: $1,205.
  • Median household income: $87,535.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 487.
  • Mean commute to work: 28 minutes.

Cities listed on the county site include Belton, Raymore, Peculiar, Pleasant Hill, Harrisonville, Archie, Drexel and Garden City. Each records its deeds in the same Harrisonville office.

More questions about Cass County, MO Recorder of Deeds

What does Cass County, MO bill for recording a deed?

State law sets $5 on page one and $3 on each added page, and a $6 user fee applies to each instrument. Instruments named in RSMo 59.330 also carry a $3 housing trust fund fee. A document that does not meet the county's formatting standards adds $25. Check the posted schedule on the county fee page before you send payment.

Can the Cass County Recorder of Deeds write or fix my deed?

No. The Recorder reviews and records documents but does not prepare or change them. The office points people to a title company or a real estate attorney. If a recorded deed needs correcting, it goes back through as a corrected recording or a re-recording with a new cover sheet, new signatures and a new acknowledgment.

How long does recording take at the Cass County recorder?

The office reports same-day to 24-hour turnaround on real estate recordings, excluding holidays and weekends. Electronic submissions through the iCounty portal can be recorded and returned in minutes for registered users. A rejected paper document restarts the clock, so check the margins and first page items before sending it.

Can I record a Cass County deed electronically?

Yes, for registered submitters. You complete an electronic recording registration packet, either with the Cass County Recorder or through iCounty, and send it to the Wall Street address in Harrisonville or to the email on the county's e-recording page. Fees can be paid by ACH through the portal, though delinquent documents are not accepted for ACH.

Does the Cass County recorder show what a house sold for?

No. Recorded real estate documents in Cass County do not carry the selling price, and the office does not give out closing details by phone. Ask the title insurance company, lender or real estate agent. The recorder can show you the recorded deed itself, its book and page and its recording date on the public computers.

Where is the Newton County Recorder of Deeds and when is it open?

The Recorder of Deeds sits in Suite 209 of the courthouse at 101 S Wood St in Neosho, MO 64850, and the phone line is (417) 451-8224. The recorder's own website says the office is on the main floor in the northeast corner of the building. The counter is staffed from 8 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon on weekdays and shuts for holidays.

Timing matters for a closing. The office accepts recordings until 3:30 pm, and anything handed in after that goes onto the books the next business day in the order received. Marriage licenses stop being issued at 3:00 pm. Mail goes to P.O. Box 604, and the email address is recorder@ncrecorder.org.

Jenny Childers holds the office. She began as a deputy recorder in 2000, became chief deputy in 2010 and started her second term as the elected recorder on January 3, 2023.

What does the Newton County recorder keep on file?

The office is the permanent record of who owns land in Newton County. It records warranty deeds, deeds of trust, releases, plats, surveys and powers of attorney, and it also holds military discharges plus state and federal tax liens.

A few limits are worth knowing before you call:

  • Staff cannot practice law, so they will not draft a deed, hand out legal forms or explain what a filed paper means.
  • The office does not produce abstracts of title or opinions on the status of a title (RSMo 59.200.1).
  • Someone else drafts the paper, whether a closing office or a lawyer; the recorder indexes it, scans it and keeps the permanent copy.

The land lies here, so the deed goes here. RSMo 442.380 directs any written conveyance of real estate to the recorder of the county where that real estate is situated.

The county fee page lists $26 for the first page of a standard document and $3 for each page after that. Because a flat $2.00 statewide increase under Senate Bill 938 took effect on August 28, 2026, call (417) 451-8224 for the figure on your invoice today.

The recorder keeps any overpayment of up to $10 so a slightly short or long check does not trigger a rejection, as long as the payment is not below the statutory fee. A document that releases or assigns several items carries $5 for each item past the first.

What must a deed look like before the Newton County recorder accepts it?

Newton's recorder can turn away a paper that fails the layout test in RSMo 59.310, or take it and add a $25 penalty. The office's format page lays out what passes.

  • Paper: 8.5 by 11, white or pale, 20 pound stock, no logos, ink on one side.
  • Text: dark ink, 8 point or bigger, with every signer's name typed under the signature.
  • Page one: a clear 3 inch band at the top for the recorder's certificate, then the title, date, grantors with their marital status, grantees, mailing addresses the statute calls for, and the legal description.
  • Side and bottom margins: three quarters of an inch.

Indexing depends on labels. The words grantor and grantee must appear next to the parties, and the situs address of a house cannot stand in for a legal description. Exempt from these rules are papers signed before 2002, military separation papers, certified copies, foreign executed documents and anything where an original party has died or lacks capacity. Rejections are returned with a stated reason.

The office lists same day recording, payment by ACH and quick correction of a rejected document among the reasons to use it.

A rejected electronic filing can be corrected and sent again without a courier run. Electronic recording rests on RSMo 59.563, which lets a recorder set an electronic format but does not force any recorder to offer one.

What is Deed Watch and why would a Newton County owner sign up?

Deed Watch is a free property fraud alert. You visit DeedWatch.com, pick Newton County, Missouri, enter and confirm an email address, then add your search criteria, such as your name or parcel. The recorder's page describes it as a free service for catching recording activity on your property.

Owners of a vacant, inherited or rented Newton County house benefit most, since nobody is at the property to notice a forged deed or a lien filed against it. The recorder also posts instructions on how to flag suspicious recording activity.

What is Newton County like for someone selling a house?

Newton County lies in the southwest corner of Missouri, is part of the Joplin metropolitan area, and has its seat in Neosho. The county was organized in 1838 and named for John Newton, a Revolutionary War hero. Land area comes to roughly 625 square miles. Residents numbered 58,648 in the 2020 count, and the federal estimate for July 2025 reads 62,263, up 6.1 percent from the April 2020 base.

Cities include Neosho, Seneca, Granby, Diamond and Fairview, and a corner of Joplin extends into the county from the north. School districts that cover Newton County addresses include Neosho R-V, East Newton County R-VI, Diamond R-IV and Seneca R-VII. The George Washington Carver National Monument is also inside the county.

With three of every four households owning their home, most Newton County deals are owner-to-buyer transfers that end at this recorder's counter.

What should I ask the recorder about a title problem on a Newton County house?

This counter cannot clear a title. The recorder is the place to confirm that a deed of trust has a recorded release, that a plat or survey for the parcel is on file, and that a tax lien has been filed or released. The format page adds that releases and assignments must cite the book and page of the paper they refer to.

For anything beyond that, such as who holds a valid claim, bring in an attorney or a title searcher. Sellers dealing with an inherited or tenant-occupied house often start with a title search to learn which recorded papers need a release before a buyer can close. Newton County also runs a delinquent tax sale each August, so a parcel with unpaid taxes can carry an extra recorded history.

Which Newton County offices matter besides the recorder?

Several county offices share the same courthouse, so one trip can cover them all. Ask each for current figures.

  • Assessor Cheryle Perkins, Suite 205, (417) 451-8228, places the value on real and personal property for tax purposes and is staffed on weekdays until 4:30.
  • Collector Jessica Crawford, Suite 203, (417) 451-8217, issues tax bills and runs the delinquent tax sale on the fourth Monday of August.
  • County Clerk Tami Owens, (417) 451-8221, is the person to ask where a valuation appeal gets filed. The county lists its Board of Equalization among boards appointed by the commission.

The collector's page states that a tax obligation is fixed on January 1 and the law gives no pro-rating, and that the current owner is responsible for taxes due. Ask your closing office how the year's bill gets split on the settlement sheet, and ask the collector what is still unpaid before you sign. Bills are mailed November 1 and turn delinquent after midnight on December 31.

Is a transfer tax collected on Newton County deeds?

None appears on the county fee page, which lists recording charges only. Ask your closing agent whether anything else is owed on your sale.

What is the cutoff for same day recording at the Neosho courthouse?

Be at the counter by 3:30 pm. Staff stay until 4:30, yet new recordings are taken only until 3:30, and later arrivals go on the record the following business day.

The recorder's site points to a name, legal description or recording reference as the way into the records, and staff cannot give legal advice. For a parcel by address, the assessor in Suite 205 at (417) 451-8228 is the better first call.

How can I send documents to the Newton County recorder without driving to Neosho?

You can mail them to P.O. Box 604 or use electronic recording through iCounty Technologies at (816) 295-1540. The office keeps up to $10 of any overpayment, so include enough to cover the fee.

What if the paper I bring does not meet the layout rules?

The recorder may reject it and send it back with the reason, or record it with the $25 nonstandard charge added to the page fees.

St Francois County by the numbers

Where does St. Francois County keep its land records?

Recorder Jay Graf's staff work out of Suite 100 on the ground level of the courthouse annex, 1 West Liberty Street, Farmington. The county suggests using the rear main parking lot entrance. The office records, maintains and archives deeds, liens, marriage licenses, surveys, plats and military discharge papers (Recorder page).

  • Phone: 573-756-2323, or 573-431-6505 then option 1 and 7.
  • Hours: weekdays, 8:00 a.m. until 4:00 p.m.
  • Cards: debit and credit are taken, and a convenience fee of at least $2.00 applies to each transaction.
  • Search: the deed index books and all recorded documents are online in Tapestry under Land Records Search. A Laredo subscription is another option; ask the office.

Federal and state tax liens and their releases are recorded in this office too, and copies can be requested in writing or in person. The county Assessor (Suite 200) and Collector (Suite 201) work in the same annex, so one trip can cover a lien check, a parcel record and a tax payoff before a sale.

What are the recording charges in Farmington?

Recording fees come from RSMo 59.310. The county's fee page adds that Senate Bill 938 brought a flat $2.00 statewide increase on August 28, 2026 for documents, marriage licenses and plats or surveys. Call for the all-in total for your page count before you drive over.

The statute text on the legislature's site is the 2022 version, so the county page is the better guide to the current schedule. If you wonder whether any transfer-related charge applies to your deed, put that question to the Recorder at 573-756-2323.

What formatting gets a deed accepted?

Under RSMo 59.310 the Recorder can turn away a paper that breaks the format rules, or take it for an extra $25. A refusal must come back with a written reason. Every document needs a legal description of the property, certified court copies included.

  • Paper: letter size, white or light colored, 20 pound stock, one side only, with nothing stapled on except what a statute requires.
  • Margins: three blank inches across the top of page one for the Recorder, and at least 3/4 inch elsewhere.
  • Type: eight point or larger, in black or dark ink, sharp enough to copy cleanly.
  • Signatures: dark ink, each with the signer's name typed, printed or stamped below.

Under that margin the county's list calls for the title of the document, its date, each grantor (labeled with the word Grantor, plus marital status), each grantee (labeled Grantee), any statutory addresses, the legal description and book and page references where they apply. A cover sheet may hold this information. Exempt from the format rules are papers signed before January 1, 2002, military separation papers, documents executed outside the United States and court judgments.

What happens when a recorded deed has an error?

It can be re-recorded, but the second filing faces the same tests as a fresh one. The county wants correct margins, legibility and first page information, a new cover sheet saying why the document is being recorded again, and a new acknowledgment from the notary.

That detail matters when a sale is close to closing. A wrong legal description or a missing grantor name can delay the title company, so have the escrow officer review the deed before anyone signs. The Recorder also offers a free Property Fraud Alert, a notification service meant to warn owners when someone records a fraudulent document that makes it look as if the filer owns your home. You can subscribe online or call the alert line at 800-728-3858.

What should sellers know about the county around Farmington?

The county lies in Missouri's Lead Belt, covers about 455 square miles and was organized December 19, 1821. Farmington serves as seat and largest city, alongside Bismarck, Bonne Terre, Desloge, Iron Mountain Lake, Leadington, Leadwood and Park Hills (Wikipedia). Public schools are run by the Bismarck R-V, Farmington R-VII, North St. Francois County R-1, St. Francois County Central R-III and West St. Francois County R-IV districts, and Mineral Area College is a two-year college in Park Hills.

QuickFacts estimates 67,809 residents for July 2025 and 29,596 housing units. The 2020 census found 66,922 people, up from 65,359 in 2010. Roughly 68.2% of households own. For 2020 to 2024 the survey reports a $169,300 typical home value, $794 typical rent and $57,477 typical household income. The county Assessor reports more than 41,075 parcels of real estate and a certified assessed value over $994 million as of 2024.

Who collects tax and holds the tax sale here?

Collector Angie K. Usery (Suite 201, 573-756-2645) takes in current and delinquent tax and runs the county tax sale on the fourth Monday of August. The 2026 sale fell on August 24. For parcels owed after June 30, only full payment was accepted, in cash, money order or cashier's check, through 4:00 p.m. on August 21 (tax sale page).

The Assessor, Eric Dugal, is in Suite 200 at 573-756-1878. The 2026 bills can be paid at the Collector's office and online. The collector's page also lists an installment plan run with EquaPay for owners whose taxes are not paid through a mortgage escrow, and a senior tax credit. The credit was adopted by the County Commission in December 2024 as Ordinance 2024-12-10-1. The next enrollment runs March 1 through May 31, 2027, in person at the Collector's office between 9:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m., and requires photo ID. Applicants must be 62 by January 1 of the base year and current on tax. The program's FAQ names December 31 as the last day to pay each year without late charges.

Does a St. Francois County senior tax credit pass to the buyer?

No. The program's FAQ says the credit stays with the eligible taxpayer's homestead and does not transfer to a new property owner or to a different home. A senior who moves and still qualifies files a new application, which sets a new base year for the new address.

The credit is the gap between a year's tax on the homestead and the tax in the base year. It is not a freeze on assessed value, so the amount can shift, and some pieces of the bill sit outside the credit by law, such as the State Blind Pension Fund and voter-approved bond levies. Delinquent tax disqualifies an applicant, trust or LLC owners must bring their documents, and both spouses on the deed are asked to apply in person. Review can take up to 30 days. For a seller this means a buyer's first bill may look different from yours, so the Collector at 573-756-2645 is the place to ask what applies to a specific parcel.

Owners who are not escrowed can also spread the year's bill over monthly drafts with EquaPay. The county describes four steps: look up your bill, create an account and pick a draft date and method (bank account or card), let EquaPay calculate payments from the time left before the due date, and finish enrollment so it pays the county on time.

More questions about St. Francois County, MO Recorder of Deeds

How do I search for a recorded deed?

Use the Land Records Search tab on the Recorder's page, which opens Tapestry and shows the deed index books and recorded documents. You can also call 573-756-2323 or visit the annex in Farmington.

When can I visit the Recorder?

Weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The county website also keeps an office closures page for holiday schedules.

Why might my deed come back unrecorded?

The usual causes are a missing legal description, a first page without the three-inch top margin, text smaller than eight point or missing grantor and grantee labels. The office must return a rejected document with the reason.

Does the Recorder accept cards?

Yes. The office takes debit and credit cards and charges a minimum $2.00 convenience fee on every transaction.

Is property tax paid to the Recorder?

No. The Collector, Angie K. Usery, bills and collects property tax at Suite 201 of the same annex building. The Recorder handles deeds, liens and plats.

What does the Franklin County Recorder of Deeds do?

The Recorder of Deeds keeps the public land record for Franklin County, Missouri. A deed that moves a house from one owner to another, and the deed of trust or release that goes with a loan, becomes part of that record once the office accepts it. The county seat is Union, and the county's home page carries a Record My Deeds link next to its tax payment and marriage license links.

Other county offices rely on what the Recorder files. The county assessor says it receives and processes more than 10,000 instruments and deeds a year from the county GIS department, and it uses them to keep ownership and parcel records current. Over 6,300 subdivisions are on file in the county. A deed that never gets recorded leaves the old owner's name on that trail.

Land titles in this county have a long paper trail. The Spanish built the log fort San Juan del Misuri at present-day Washington between 1796 and 1803, Daniel Boone settled the area from 1799, the county was organized in 1818, and German families began arriving in numbers in 1833.

Ask the office directly for its current room, hours and accepted payment types before you travel, and ask whether your title company can file for you.

Why does a recorded deed matter for a Franklin County sale?

Franklin County is a big, growing place for a Missouri county. The Census Bureau estimates 108,090 people in July 2025 across 922.65 square miles of land, about 113.5 people per square mile as of 2020. There are 43,036 households with 2.44 people each, and 90.1 percent of residents stayed in the same house over the prior year.

Homes here carry real costs. Median monthly owner costs are $1,442 with a mortgage and $505 without one, while median gross rent is $893. The county issued 794 building permits in 2025, so new houses are a steady part of the market.

A recorded deed is the proof of ownership for the next buyer's lender, and for the assessor's notices. Under RSMo 137.180 an assessor who raises a value must notify the record owner, so a buyer whose deed is not on file may see mail go to the former owner.

What format rules must a document meet before the Recorder accepts it?

RSMo 59.310 lets a Missouri recorder of deeds refuse a document that does not meet the page rules. A county can still record a nonconforming document for an extra $25. These are the state's main format rules:

  • Pages are printed on one side only and are not permanently bound or on a continuous form
  • Type is at least eight-point, in black or dark ink, and clear enough to copy
  • Paper is white or light colored, at least 20-pound weight, with no watermarks
  • Signatures are in dark ink with the name typed, printed or stamped beneath
  • The top margin is at least three inches on the first page, kept clear for the Recorder's certification, and every other margin is at least three-quarters of an inch

Documents signed before 2002, military separation papers, papers signed outside the United States, certified copies and court judgments are exempt from these format rules. A rejected paper comes back to the person who presented it with the reason it was refused.

What must the first page of a deed show?

Below the three-inch top margin on page one, state law asks for the items that identify the transaction. If they do not fit, the first page must say where in the document they appear.

  • The title of the document and its date
  • The names of all grantors with their marital status, and the names of all grantees
  • Any statutory addresses
  • The legal description of the property
  • Book and page references, where a statute calls for them

The legal description is the line most often copied wrongly. Copy it from the vesting deed or the title commitment, not from a tax bill, and have the title company read it before signing. A mistake there can mean a corrective deed and a second round of fees.

What are the Missouri recording fees at the Franklin County Recorder?

These are the statute's base amounts. Under those base rates a five-page deed comes to $17. Ask the Franklin County office for the total on your page count before you mail a check.

Which taxes should be settled before a Franklin County deed is recorded?

Recording does not clear property tax. The Franklin County Collector, Doug Trentmann, is in Room 103 at 400 E Locust in Union and answers at 636-583-6353. The Collector bills for the county and 64 other taxing entities, so one parcel can owe to several of them on a single statement.

Taxes are due by December 31. After that they are delinquent, and the state adds an 18 percent penalty on the year's delinquency under RSMo 140.100. Delinquent land is offered for sale on the fourth Monday in August under RSMo 140.150, and the owner can pay what is owed up to the moment of the sale.

A purchaser who buys a house less than 30 days after the county mailed the tax statement may take an assessment appeal straight to the State Tax Commission, which says so in its guidance. In every other case the Board of Equalization comes first, and its filing date is the second Monday in July.

How do I record a deed after selling a Franklin County house?

Many sales close through a title company, which can prepare the deed, collect the fee and file it. For a private sale or a family transfer, have the deed drafted to the page rules above, check the legal description and then deliver it to the Recorder. Keep the recorded copy, since that is the proof the transfer went through.

Before closing, tell the title company which tax years are open and whether any lien, such as a judgment or a mechanic's claim, sits on the property. If the house was inherited or has tenants, ask the title company what has to be recorded first, and what a cash buyer will pay for at closing.

Give the buyer a clear contact for the Collector and the Assessor.

More questions about Franklin County, MO Recorder of Deeds

Where do I record a deed in Franklin County, Missouri?

At the county Recorder of Deeds. The county website's home page has a Record My Deeds link. Contact the office for its room, hours and payment methods, or have your title company file for you.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Franklin County?

The statute's base fee is $5 for the first page and $3 for each later page. The office can quote the full total for your page count.

Why did the Recorder reject my deed?

Usually a format problem. RSMo 59.310 requires a three-inch top margin, dark ink, at least eight-point type and the first-page details. A rejected document is returned with a written reason, and a nonconforming one can be recorded for an extra $25.

Does recording a deed pay off property taxes?

No. Taxes are owed to the Franklin County Collector at 636-583-6353 and are due by December 31. Unpaid land can go to the fourth Monday in August sale.

Which Franklin County cities does the Recorder cover?

The whole county. That includes Union, Washington, Pacific, Sullivan, New Haven, St. Clair, Berger and Gerald, and unincorporated areas such as Gray Summit and Villa Ridge.

Documents since May 1963 are in digital form, and anything older sits in books at the office. You can come in, call or email to get a copy, and copies cost $1 per page, with an extra $2 when the copy is emailed.

Missouri law makes recording matter. Under RSMo 442.400 an instrument is not valid against anyone except the parties and people with actual notice until it is deposited with the recorder. A signed deed that never reaches the Recorder leaves the buyer exposed, so confirm the title company files it right after closing.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Ray County?

The Ray County fee schedule lists $26 for the first page of a recorded document and $3 for each additional page. That total is higher than the $5 first page and $3 added page named in the base fee statute, RSMo 59.310, so bring the county's posted figure when you budget for closing.

Source: Ray County Recorder of Deeds. The office takes checks, cash and debit or credit cards for recordings and copies.

How do I get a deed recorded in Ray County?

Take it to the office, mail it, or file it electronically. For a mailed deed, the Recorder asks you to include a self-addressed stamped envelope so the original comes back to you. E-recording runs through iCounty at raymo.icounty.com, and iCounty's number listed on the county page is 816-295-1540.

Most sellers never file anything themselves, because the title company or closing attorney sends the deed and the lender's release. Even so, a few practical steps help:

  • Check that every signature has the printed name under it, as RSMo 59.310 requires.
  • Keep type no smaller than 8 point and make the page legible enough to copy cleanly.
  • Remember that an oversized page or an added sheet for the recorder's stamp counts as an extra page.
  • Ask the closing agent for the recording date and book or document number after filing.

For a quitclaim, a transfer on death deed or a release, ask a title company or a Missouri attorney to draft the document before you bring it in.

Can I protect my Ray County property from deed fraud?

Yes. The Recorder points owners to a free property fraud alert at deedwatch.com, which notifies you when a document is filed under your name. If you get an alert for something you did not sign, call the Recorder at 816-776-4500.

The office cannot remove a recorded document from the public record without a court order signed by a judge. An owner who believes a forged deed was filed should speak with an attorney and can also report it to the Ray County Sheriff or the police department in the city involved. Signing up before you list a vacant or inherited house takes a few minutes and costs nothing.

What is Ray County like for someone selling a house?

Ray County lies in northwest Missouri and is part of the Kansas City metro area. It was organized on November 16, 1820, covers 574 square miles and has Richmond as its seat and largest city. Routes 10, 13 and 210 run through it, and it borders Caldwell, Carroll, Lafayette, Jackson, Clay and Clinton counties.

The Census Bureau counted 23,158 residents in 2020 and estimates 23,398 for July 1, 2025. Its QuickFacts page gives a median owner-occupied home value of $198,800 for 2020 to 2024, an owner-occupied rate of 77.3 percent, median gross rent of $782 and a mean commute of 34.3 minutes. Median household income is $74,573, and 66 building permits were recorded in 2025.

Besides Richmond, the county's cities include Camden, Crystal Lakes, Excelsior Springs (mostly in Clay County), Fleming, Hardin, Henrietta, Lawson, Orrick and Wood Heights. School districts here are Richmond R-XVI, Orrick R-XI, Lawson R-XIV and Hardin-Central C-2, so a deed's legal description and the tax bill will show which one applies.

How do I get a copy of a recorded deed in Ray County?

Visit the office, phone it or email it. The Recorder charges $1 per page for a copy of a deed, and an emailed copy adds $2 on top of the per-page charge. Certification costs $1 per document, which matters when a lender or court wants a stamped copy.

Plan on a short wait for anything recorded before May 1963, because those items are kept in books rather than as digital images. A copy of a plat or survey is $5. Sellers who cannot find their own deed usually need one for the legal description, and ordering it early keeps the title search moving.

How does a recorded deed connect to property tax in Ray County?

The recorded deed tells the assessor who owns a parcel, and the owner on January 1 is the one assessed. Missouri values residential real property at 19 percent of true value under RSMo 137.115, and new assessed values are set as of January 1 of each odd-numbered year, which makes 2027 the next one.

Ray County's QuickFacts median home value of $198,800 gives a rough sense of the base before that percentage is applied. For the actual bill, parcel number and levy district, contact the Ray County Assessor and Collector, since the Recorder's office records ownership and does not collect tax. Missouri's tax calendar runs to December 31 for payment, so a house that sells in the fall deserves a tax check before the deed is signed.

What else should I settle before closing on a Ray County house?

Property tax status comes next after recording. Ask the Ray County Collector for the current bill and any delinquent years, and have the title company pay off tax liens or unpaid bills from the proceeds. The recording step only works smoothly when the title is clean.

  • Pull any old deed of trust that was paid but never released, since the release must be recorded too.
  • Order copies of recent deeds if the legal description looks wrong.
  • If the seller died, expect the title company to want probate paperwork on file before a deed is signed.
  • Sellers who need to close quickly on an inherited or tenant-occupied house sometimes take a cash offer, which still requires a recorded deed.

Questions about what a document means for your sale belong with your attorney or closing agent, since the Recorder's office files instruments and does not advise on them.

What does it cost to record a deed in Ray County?

$26 for the first page and $3 for each added page, according to the Recorder's posted fees. Plats and surveys are priced separately, and the office accepts cash, checks and cards.

Where is the Ray County Recorder of Deeds office?

It is in Richmond, the county seat. Call 816-776-4500 to confirm hours and where to mail a document before you send anything.

Yes. E-recording is available through iCounty at raymo.icounty.com, and the county lists 816-295-1540 as the iCounty contact. Title companies commonly use it for closings.

To 1820. Records from May 1963 forward are digital, and older items are kept in books at the Recorder's office.

Call the Recorder at 816-776-4500 and see an attorney. The Recorder cannot remove a filed document without a court order, so a judge must act. You can also report suspected fraud to the Ray County Sheriff.

Webster County by the numbers

Where is the Webster County Recorder of Deeds?

The Recorder of Deeds works from Room 16 of the Webster County Courthouse in Marshfield. The Recorder's own page gives the street as 101 N Crittenden, with a mailing address of P.O. Box 546, Marshfield, MO 65706, and the phone is 417-859-5882. Other county pages print the courthouse as 101 S Crittenden, so call before you mail anything or drive in.

Stacy Atkison is the elected Recorder, and Sarah Bodine serves as Deputy Recorder. The office's stated mission is to record and preserve land records accurately and quickly. It also issues marriage licenses and records and copies military discharge papers (DD-214).

Marshfield sits 1,490 feet above sea level and is the highest county seat in Missouri. The present courthouse, faced in Carthage marble, was built from 1939 to 1941 and is the county's third.

Marshfield itself was laid out in 1856 on land given by C.F. Dryden and W.T. and B.F.T. Burford. Until a courthouse was built, county business was conducted at Hazelwood, where Joseph W. McClurg, later a governor of Missouri, ran a general store.

One caution about timing. Missouri raised recorder fees by a flat $2.00 on August 28, 2026 under Senate Bill 938, a change the Stone County Recorder announced and that appears in the amended text of RSMo 59.319. Ask the Webster office whether the $26 price on its page already includes that increase.

What layout does a Webster County deed have to follow?

Webster County lists three layout standards: a three inch margin at the top of the first page, three-quarters of an inch on the remaining sides, and letter-size white paper. A deed outside those lines is treated as non-standard and costs the extra $25.

State law adds content requirements. Under RSMo 59.330, a deed has to carry a legal description of the land and a mailing address for one grantee, and the Recorder may not file it without them. Closing agents normally prepare the deed with these items in place, but a seller preparing a deed without a title company should check each one before mailing it.

How do you search Webster County land records online?

The Recorder's online document search went live on February 1, 2023. The site is titled Document Search for the Index of Recorded Deeds. A visitor registers as a new user, and the account can then search and buy copies of recorded documents. Subscription levels run from free to several paid options, depending on use.

Searching in person at the Recorder's office in Room 16 is free to the public. The county's page for the service gives the paid online plan as $200 per month, with a limit of 300 documents viewed or printed. An owner checking a single deed can start with the free route.

Webster County also points owners to DeedWatch.com, described as a free service.

What else does the Recorder issue besides deed recordings?

Marriage licenses are a regular part of the counter work. Both parties must appear with valid government identification, and each person has to supply a Social Security number and the month and year any prior marriage ended. An online application is optional and speeds things up.

  • Certified copy: $9, the document used to change a name on a driver's license or Social Security card.
  • Validity: 30 days, and the ceremony must take place in Missouri.

The office also records and issues copies of DD-214 military discharge papers.

Which Webster County offices handle a home sale?

A sale touches several offices inside the same courthouse.
